utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Steven Todorovic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) First of all, for the benefit of the two parties, I should like to say that Judge Richard May is very sick today. He has gone down with flu and he apologises for his absence. I am, therefore, going to ask the parties, that is the Prosecution and the Defence, first of all to introduce themselves, and then I would like to hear their view, that is whether they agree that the Chamber sit in this composition, that is Judge Patrick Robinson and myself, but first let me ask you to introduce yourselves, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASLUND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Can the accused follow in a language they understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No? There appears to be a translation problem. Let us check with the booth, please. Can you hear us now? Can the accused understand and follow in a language that they understand? There's the English translation for the parties. Are you able to follow the English translation? Legal officer, can someone assist Judge Robinson, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: One, two, three. One, two, three. English booth? One, two, three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The Prosecutor, please. Will you please -- let's hear the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASLUND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am Anne Haslund. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor, and on my right side is Ms. Nancy Paterson, and on my left side is Ms. Mary MacFadyen, and there is Carmela Annik-Janvier, our case manager. We do not object that only two Judges participate in this hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Defence counsel. Microphone, please. It's not switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I always seem to have a problem with this microphone. With regard to the inquiry by the Court as to the composition of the panel, I would like to consult with other Defence counsel before expressing a position, and, therefore, after the parties and their counsel introduce themselves, I would like to caucus with Defence counsel if that request would be granted by the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That's perfect. Let me ask the other Defence counsel to introduce themselves and then we will give you a few minutes to consult amongst each other before we ask for your answer. Will the other Defence counsel introduce themselves, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. AVRAMOVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, my name is Branislav Avramovic, Defence counsel for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, my name is Borislav Pisarevic, Defence counsel for the accused Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm Igor Pantelic, Defence counsel for Miroslav Tadic. Although I'm not so in good shape these days because of the flu but still I'm here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I'm Saint Just from the Paris bar, and I'm co-counsel of Mr. Pantelic for Miroslav Tadic, and this is the first time that I appear in your court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you and welcome. At the request of Mr. Brashich, you wish to consult with the other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I would request only two or three minutes, and rather than having the Court be disturbed, perhaps I and co-counsel could just go to the robing room for one minute and exchange views and come right back in without disturbing the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, please do that. We have -- we shall have a two-minute break to give Defence counsel time to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I have consulted with co-counsel -- Defence counsel, and the position that I take on behalf of the defendant Todorovic, is that all motions now pending before the Court I will agree as to the composure of the panel, except for two motions I have made with regard to the defendant Todorovic, and that is the motion to sever and the motion for an evidentiary hearing on the arrest and detection of my client. I would like to have a full bench with regard to those two motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Brashich. I'm going to consult with my colleague. The Chamber accepts your request. Therefore, we're going to deal with all the pending motions that I'm going to refer to in a moment, with the exception of two motions, the motion for a severance and the motion on evidentiary hearing on the arrest, regarding which we will have another hearing later on with the full composition of the Chamber to -- in response to your request. The motions -- the total number of pending motions are 15. We have four motions submitted by the Prosecution, the Office of the Prosecution, and eleven motions submitted by the Defence, basically by the Defence of Mr. Todorovic. I would suggest -- of course, we received the motions and virtually all the responses to those motions yesterday evening. I would, therefore, suggest that we first hear the motions of the Prosecution in the following order: The two motions on judicial notice on the character of the conflict, that is judicial notice regarding the character of the conflict --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Judge is repeating in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) -- and judicial notice of adjudicated facts, which, in my view, could be heard together. I shall first give the floor to the Office of the Prosecution regarding these two motions before hearing the defence. After that we will proceed in the following order: We will address the motion on the admission of evidence, followed by the motion on the conflict of interest, which was also submitted by the Prosecution, and then I will give the floor to Defence counsel and we will proceed with the motion submitted by the Defence. Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The way the Court has suggested -- or ordered, could I possibly suggest that the first order of business would be the conflict of interest of one of the Defence counsel? If that is decided subsequently, then we would have a defendant without counsel present in these proceedings. So if I could respectfully suggest that we clear up that matter first, as to whether or not there is a conflict with one of the Defence counsel. And assuming that the Court rules that there is no conflict, then we could proceed with the other motions. This is only a suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The view of the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASLUND
utterances.text: The Prosecution will leave it to the Court to decide in what order the motions should be orally argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let us begin then with the motion on the conflict of interest submitted by Madam Haslund, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASLUND
utterances.text: As the Prosecution is represented by three lawyers. I shall inform the Court and my learned colleagues on the defence bar that we have divided the tasks among us, and Ms. Nancy Paterson will represent -- will represent the Prosecutor in the oral argument on the international conflict and the adjudicated facts. Thank you. If Your Honour decides that the motion submitted by the Prosecution on the conflict of interest should be dealt with first, it will be Ms. Mary MacFadyen who will represent the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ms. Mary MacFadyen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm Canadian but English speaking, so I'm going to speak in English if you don't mind. (In English) The Prosecution motion asking for the Court to determine if there is indeed a conflict of interest regarding Mr. Pisarevic's -- Mr. Pisarevic's representation of Mr. Zaric was filed on December 16th. There was only one response from the Defence counsel, and that was on January 21st, 1999 from Mr. Pisarevic. Some recent developments since the Defence motion was filed should be brought to the notice of the court, and that is with respect to the footnote number 23 in the Prosecution's motion, which indicates that Mr. Pisarevic is aided by Mr. Nenad Borcilovic. I understand that he was registered with the Registry as a legal assistant until January 29th of this year, at which time he was replaced by a Mr. Lasarevic, I believe, or Jaravic. I'm not exactly sure what his first name is, the Registry didn't give me that. It appears that he was replaced as a legal assistant for Mr. Pisarevic very shortly after the Status Conference on January 21st, 1999. It is the Prosecution's contention that Mr. Pisarevic, even if all of the parties present do not intend to call him as a witness at this time, is likely to be a witness because of his position and knowledge of the facts. Those are set out in the Prosecution's motion, and I will just summarise them. There are four matters that Mr. Pisarevic would have personal knowledge of and which he might be called as a witness, most likely in rebuttal if not in cross-examination or in direct, but if, in fact, all the parties agree that he wouldn't be called as a witness, then it would be most likely in rebuttal, and that is with respect to his relationship with the victim-witness Mr. Sulejman Tihic. According to Mr. Tihic, a statement which has been presented to the Defence and the court in the confirmation materials, Mr. Tihic, on the night of the invasion of Bosanski Samac on April the 17th, 1992, stayed at the house of Mr. Pisarevic, and, in fact, talked to him about whether or not he should surrender. Mr. Pisarevic apparently phoned Simo Zaric and Blagoje Simic both of whom are co-accused in this matter, and according to the witness Mr. Tihic, Blagoje Simic demanded that Mr. Tihic surrender, but Mr. Zaric told him not to. However, Mr. Pisarevic later on accompanied Mr. Tihic to the police station where, in fact, he was arrested by Mr. Todorovic -- well, he was presented to Mr. Todorovic, and he was taken there at gun point. So, in fact, Mr. Pisarevic is witness to a conversation that was, as far as the Prosecution is aware, between himself and two co-accused. Mr. Tihic can only testify as to what he heard on one side of the conversation. It has been indicated in the response by Mr. Pisarevic to the motion that, in fact, everything that Mr. Tihic says is in dispute. I suggest, therefore, that the only evidence of what really occurred in that conversation either comes from either of the accused or Mr. Pisarevic. If neither of the accused wish to testify for any other reasons, they would be forced to testify in order to give the Court full knowledge of this conversation, which I suggest goes to the credibility of Mr. Tihic, the witness. One of the important witnesses in the Prosecution's case. The second point that would indicate Mr. Pisarevic is -- his knowledge is of importance with respect to his position on conflict is that prior to the invasion on April 17th, 1992, he was the president of the Party of Democratic Changes, which the Prosecution hopes to show was connected with the Serbian party. He apparently had advance knowledge, according to the Prosecution's witnesses, of the invasion. And since in some of the counts in the indictment that is before the court today it's indicated that the planning and instigation, the commission of persecutions and deportations as a result of much of the planning that occurred through party before the invasion, I would suggest that Mr. Pisarevic's personal knowledge of what went on would be of great value to the Prosecution, if not the Defence. Thirdly, there is a witness, Omar Nalic, whose name was disclosed to the Defence on January 21st at the Status Conference and also in this motion, December the 16th, who claims to have had a forced confession extracted from him by Simo Zaric. It was later used, it was later indicated to him that it would be used, in a Serbian military Court in Jelina, at which Mr. Pisarevic was also present. The victim statement is a little vague on this point, it's quite true. Mr. Pisarevic at that time indicated that he would either represent Mr. Nalic or find someone to represent him. He then disappeared from the scene. As a consequence of this military Court in Jelina, Mr. Nalic was convicted of armed insurrection. Fourthly, Mr. Pisarevic was a witness himself to an important event in the Prosecution's case, and that is with respect to the counts charging the beating of Hasan Bisic, Muhamed Bisic, and Perica Misic. According to the witness statements, they were beaten by Mr. Milan Simic, and following that beating, Mr. Simic took Hasan Bisic and Perica Mesic out of detainment for an evening of entertainment at his office. On the way back from his office, Mr. Hasan Bisic and Perica Misic saw Mr. Pisarevic, whom they knew before, because he was a prominent citizen of Bosanski Samac, on the street. It is the Prosecution's contention, and certainly would be that that is conclusory of the witness statements, that Mr. Pisarevic may have been able to see what condition these two witnesses were in at the time, or even who they were with, in some way corroborating their testimony. I would suggest that in this particular case, Mr. Pisarevic's evidence, unless there is another witness who can testify as to the same thing, is essential. With respect to this Court being asked to decide if there is a conflict of interest, it is not the usual course of events that a Court is asked to determine whether counsel in a matter before it suffers from a conflict of interest; but in this case there is no international bar association which can sanction any participant in this particular Court. In fact, there is a code of professional ethics set out by the Tribunal, and it indicates that in fact, no conflicts of interest will be tolerated. According to -- according to page 10 of the Defence motion on conflicts, Article 9 (ii) of the Professional Ethics Code indicates that when conflicts arise -- sorry; in the course of representing a client, counsel must exercise all care to ensure that no conflict of interest arises. And under 9(v), where a conflict of interest arises Article 9(v) provides that the counsel must promptly and fully each potentially affected client of the and nature and extent of the conflict and either take all steps necessary to remove the conflict or obtain the full and informed consent of all potentially affected clients to--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: -- So long as counsel is able to fulfil all other obligations under this code. Under 9(i) of the Code of Professional Conduct, which appears on page 13 of the Prosecution's motion, counsel owes a duty of loyalty to his or her client. Counsel must at all times act in the best interests of the client and must put those interests before their own interests or those of any other person. In article 9(iii)(C) also on page 13 of the Prosecution's motion, it indicates that the counsel's professional judgement on behalf of the client will be or may be reasonably expected to be adversely affected by the counsel's responsibilities to or interests in a third party. Therefore I would suggest that Mr. Pisarevic's personal knowledge and dealings with certain of the coaccused, and of the victim/witnesses and his knowledge of the party which is personal to him, would affect his judgement with respect to his client and also with respect to his cross-examination of the victim/witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ms. McFadyen, I forgot to specify, and I'm doing it now, perhaps -- I hope it is not too late, to the extent to which we have the documents, either of the Prosecution or the Defence, as you know, the rule is that during the hearing, we refer to the substance; that is, the points that have not already been made in the motions. I'm drawing your attention to this to say that the chamber would like the arguments to be limited to five or to ten minutes on each side. I will finish very soon. I'm not trying to prevent you from admitting any of your arguments, but I'm just asking you to focus on the essential. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: The last point that I would like to make, then, in fact, is that Mr. Pisarevic may argue that in fact the accused has the right to a counsel of his choice. I would only signal Your Honour's attention to the European Human Rights Commission convention which indicates, at page 17 of the Prosecution's motion, the right to defend one's self through assistance of one's own choosing is not an absolute right, but limited by the right of the state to make regulations concerning the appearance of lawyers before courts. The state has full discretion to exclude lawyers from appearing before courts. Those were all the points that the Prosecution wants to bring to your attention; thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ms. McFadyen, you quoted Article 9 that we have in front of us, and that you used in your motion to which you have referred, which speaks about the duty of counsel. That is Article 9(i), is as follows. Just a moment; I still haven't put my question to you. You spoke about the absence of an international bar association. In your opinion, does this Tribunal, our Tribunal, have the jurisdiction, according to its statute and its Rules of Procedure and the code of ethics, to take a decision and eliminate or prevent an attorney from defending an accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: This matter, namely conflict of interest, presented to the Tribunal by a Defence counsel, is before the Tribunal as we speak in the Jelisic case. It is another type of conflict of interest but in fact the Tribunal is being asked at the same time to rule on a conflict of interest, because of the fact that they have to be the final arbiter of the code of professional ethics in the Tribunal, and their own law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. MacFadyen. Judge Patrick Robinson has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. MacFadyen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the chamber is to determine this question of a conflict, might it not be the case that in view of the submissions that have been made by the attorney you may have a conflict as to facts, and would that not require a determination by the chamber as to those facts, where there is a dispute as to the facts? Would that not require an evidentiary hearing? Is this going to require a hearing? Would you like to address the question whether it would not be more appropriate for the chamber to deal with this question if and when it arises during the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the Rules actually deal with this question, and that is that they indicate that where there is no dispute in matters of facts then it makes no difference that the counsel representing an accused before the Tribunal has a conflict of interests. But where there is dispute of facts, then that causes a conflict of interest; that is not possible before the Tribunal. I would suggest because of Mr. Pisarevic's response, he indicates in a couple of points at least, if not all four, that those facts are in dispute. Therefore, I would suggest that, in fact, the very fact that there's a dispute is enough, without going into the actual facts themselves and what is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (No interpretation).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask your honour to turn his microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Pisarevic, my microphone was not on. I'm giving you the floor now. Excuse me; the same rule applies. Please limit yourself to the amount of time which is given to you; that is about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I do appreciate your remark, and I fully understand it and I will do my best to adapt my intervention to that time limit. However, in view of the fact that we are dealing here with a very serious issue, I'm convinced that you will understand me if I do overstep that time limit. First of all, let me express my deepest gratitude to this Tribunal for providing me with an opportunity to address this issue, to express my position regarding the Prosecutor's motion about the conflict of interest involving myself personally and the interests of my client, Mr. Simo Zaric, and also possible conflict of interest with other co-accused Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and Mr. Milan Simic and Todorovic. Your Honours, I have already submitted my written response to remove me as Defence counsel of Mr. Simo Zaric. However, I feel the need to, further on, express my position regarding the potential conflict of interest. In view of the protection of interests and rights of Mr. Zaric, his right to have a fair trial, my conscience and my professional ethics demand that I express my position regarding all relevant issues mentioned in the motion of the Prosecution. I do appreciate the concern of the Prosecutor and I do appreciate the wish to have -- to secure a fair trial to the accused Mr. Simo Zaric. I also appreciate the wish of the Prosecution to point to the possible consequences of the Trial Chamber which may arise during the proceedings. I'm placing a lot of effort -- I've been doing this for this past four years, to make sure that my client, Mr. Simo Zaric, receives a fair trial, and with that objective in mind, as early as April 1996, a long time ago, therefore, I, together with the approval of Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic, made direct contact with the investigators of the OTP and with the legal advisor Ms. Nancy Paterson in person. We met in the town of Orasje which is within the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, we've been in contact for the past four years, and I believe that we've had a very good co-operation throughout that time, and I also think that the results of that co-operation can be seen from the voluntary surrender of Mr. Tadic, Mr. Zaric and Mr. Simic. They are surrendered to the competence of the International Tribunal. Our co-operation was emphasised by the Prosecutor throughout the preliminary proceedings, and we are still endeavouring to promote that co-operation so much as it is, of course, in the interests of our clients and in the interest of the Defence. The Prosecutor has mentioned a number of facts. In their view these facts are in dispute, but I'm afraid that they have been erroneously presented. The allegations of the Prosecution that I am a citizen of the town of Samac are true. I was born in Samac, I completed my education there. I went to the university in Sarajevo, and in 1972 I was an intern Judge in Samac and the president of the Municipal Court in Samac, and I've been working as attorney at law since 1980. I'm still doing the same job in the town of Samac. It is also true that I am very well-known person both as a lawyer and as a politician. It is true that I was president of the Social Democratic Party in the municipality of Samac. I was a member of the parliament which was established after the first multi-party elections in 1990. At that time, as an MP, and together with other members of my party, we were representing the only opposition party in the then parliament which was dominated by the HDZ, SDS and SDA in coalition. My participation in the government was inexistent at that time, both de jure and de facto, except for my political activities within the Social Democratic Party, which were most of all in favour of peace and fighting against war. It is true that certain witnesses which have been mentioned have been my clients. I represented them before state and judiciary organs in various proceedings. It is also true that many witnesses were my colleagues -- are still my colleagues, professionally speaking, and they're also my friends. It's also true that during the relevant times during the conflict I was in Samac all the time, and it is true that I was a member of the army of the Republika Srpska until I was wounded on the 20th of September, 1992. After treatment I went back to the army and I was fulfilling various duties and tasks until 1996. As regards my assistance to Mr. Tihic, I can say the following: It is not true that Mr. Tihic came to see me at my house. If one reads very carefully the statement given by Mr. Tihic, it follows -- it will become apparent that I myself went to see Mr. Tihic, in my car, I went to get him and his wife, and it is not true that he spent night at my place. That occurred later on, on the next day. The idea was simply to provide assistance to Mr. Tihic. I didn't want him to experience any troubles. It is also erroneous that I talked to Mr. Zaric and Mr. Blagoje Simic as the Prosecutor has indicated. It was Mr. Tihic first who established contact with them. It is true that I myself, I also talked to them, but it was with the purpose of preventing a sort of major -- more serious conflict in the town of Samac. However, that conflict was already looming in the town. It is not true that I escorted Mr. Tihic to the police station. Mr. Tihic and myself were taken, both of us, to the police station. All this, if the Prosecution made any effort to read it more carefully, can be found in the statement of Mr. Tihic and in the recollections of Mr. Tihic that have been provided to us as discovery material. It is also true that I talked to Mr. Tihic when he came to see me the next night, but we were discussing the possibility of what can be done so that we can prevent a conflict. Further, it is not true that I was the only witness of the arrest of myself and Mr. Tihic. Witnesses will be called before this Tribunal, witnesses that have been proposed and who were also eyewitnesses to the incident, and they will be given an opportunity to discuss this issue. As regards Mr. Tihic's claim that I had sided with Serbs, well, I believe this is just his personal opinion. However, the fact is not true, because I was fiercely opposed to any nationalism, regardless of the ethnic community it was coming from, because nationalism could be seen in all three ethnic communities and generated by all three nationalistic parties. I did not participate in the government, and later on it was obvious that we had no influence in the conflict, and we didn't have any influence in the Republika Srpska and in Bosnia-Herzegovina in general. Everything that happened happened through the participation of the parties in power. And I want to make one thing clear before this Trial Chamber. I am a Serb and I am a Serb patriot. However, I'm not a nationalist. I'm not a chauvinist as the Prosecutor has attempted to describe me. I didn't know about the attack on Bosanski Samac. If I had known about the impending attack I would have taken my family away. This was done by a number of Serbs and Muslims. You can see for yourself -- you can see about that from the statement of Mr. Tihic. I didn't have any contacts with the offices of the JNA, except one contact which I had to establish under the orders of my party, and it was for the purpose of protecting the population of Bosanski Samac. As regards Article 9, when Prosecution is talking about my contacts with Omer Nalic, I have to say the following: Only certain segments have been picked up from the statement of Omer Nalic which do not paint the right picture of our conflict. It is true that I was at the military court. It is true that I was in contact with Mr. Nalic, but I had come there upon his request. He wanted to see me and I wanted to assist him both morally and in very concrete terms. He did sign a power of attorney for me so that I could come there, so that I could appear, but I did not take part in the proceedings. Nalic himself said that it was a farce. It is true I was at Batkovic on one occasion but the purpose of my visit was to take medicine to Mr. Nalic. I can only say how I managed to get there. I was seen by some people from Samac and I may have said that I would like them to go back to Samac, but not as prisoners but as free citizens. I didn't see any statement given by Mr. Omer Nalic in Bjeljina either to Simo Zaric, or to the Court in Bjeljina in general. I just want to say that it is not true that Mr. Omer Nalic was convicted by the Court in Bjeljina for the charge of armed insurrection. It is true I was not a disinterested observer of the war, because I advocated a cessation of the war and I placed all my intellectual and moral abilities to that interest and I was one of the founding members, together with Mr. Simo Zaric together with the Republika Srpska presided by Zivko Radicic and he is a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a member of the executive council of the government of Republika Srpska. It is true that I said hello to Misic and Bisic. It was dark, it was during the night. It is not true that I was wearing a uniform. Even if I had been wearing a uniform, I don't think that that by itself is something wrong. At that time an army of Republika Srpska was in existence, and the claim that that army had occupied the town is erroneous because the army was established on the 20th of May, 1992 and the takeover occurred on the 18th of April, 1992. Why does the Prosecution claim that after the beating up I saw Mr. Perica Misic and Hasan Bicic. That is absolutely not true. They needed to read a little more carefully the documents and their statements. I saw them several days later. It was night when I saw them, I greeted the people, I asked them how are you, they said fine. I didn't examine them to see whether they had any injuries or -- that could be seen. However, in a certain place in the motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just a moment, please. The Chamber is prepared to hear you, but within the limits that I have indicated, and that is that we are discussing a conflict of interest and not pleading your own case, so please bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour, I shall do my best. However, if Mr. Zaric trusts me as his Defence counsel, the Defence counsel of his choice, allow me to say that it is Zaric who is more concerned than the Prosecution. Wherever I was and whatever I saw, I had to see and do because I was living there, and there is no need for me to testify about those facts. All this points to the conclusion that not one of the accused will call me as a Defence witness. As for the Prosecution and its intimation that it might call me as a witness, I think it will not be useful, bearing in mind that I have 90 per cent of the documents of the Prosecution and I'm deeply involved in the defence of Mr. Zaric. If the Prosecution were, however, to call me as a witness, I will ask the Court to relieve me of that obligation because of my duty to keep silent about all the facts I have learnt in the course of the Defence. I have nothing to defend myself against. My conscience is clear. If the Prosecution feels that there is anything envisaged by the Statute of the Tribunal on the basis which it can charge me, let it do so. If the Prosecution is concerned about Mr. Zaric's defence, whether it will be of an appropriate quality, I suggest that it leave that decision to Mr. Zaric himself, who is certainly more interested in having a fair and just trial in order to be acquitted of the charges than the Prosecution is concerned. If there were any indication of a conflict of interest between me and my counsel, rest assured that I myself would withdraw from this duty and I would not need any warning on the part of the Court or the Prosecution. I would do the same if I saw any conflict of interest with any one of the accused. My duty as counsel is to assist my client in the preparation of his defence in accord a witness the rules and regulations and in the interests of justice. I must underline that I am the elected counsel of Mr. Zaric and I think it is his basic right to choose his counsel. No one has the right to deprive the defendant of that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me. We know that. You've already put that into writing, that it was the right of the accused to choose his counsel. Would I like to ask you whether you are familiar with Rule 16 of the Code of Conduct for counsel before the International Tribunal. That is on the 10th of June, 1997, in Article 12 it says counsel does not plead in a room which he would be called to appear as a witness unless his testimony deals with a point which is not being challenged or whether his disqualification would cause for substantial prejudice to his client. The counsel, I repeat, does not argue in a trial where he would probably be called to appear as a witness. The conflict, as Judge Robinson has recalled, there was an answer given to this. There may be a differentiation made about the interpretation of the facts, that is different between you and the Prosecutor. According to your writing, we saw that and you don't have to repeat it to us, we are being assure. But there are facts that you do recognise, that you acknowledge, even though you analyse them differently. It happens. That has been clearly established before this Trial Chamber. And I said clearly established that there may be a potential conflict of interest insofar -- and the Prosecutor developed this point in her request, that -- and in detail, where at one point you may be called to trial in order to testify, because as you acknowledge yourself, you were involved in the facts and in the events in question in this case. It is understood that if you are called to testify, you will find yourself in a situation which you yourself either under review, or re-examination, or cross-examination, or direct-examination you may put yourself into a very uncomfortable position since you will have to speak and answer questions about events that you were a part of yourself. This is what the Tribunal would hope to avoid. Therefore, we would like to avoid this type of situation, and it would be better for it to be settled right now in the interests of the accused. Of course, it would be better that it be settled now than later, once we have begun the trial. It would be better than the question of a conflict of interest, and you understand what I'm saying, be settled before the trial begins, and that is at the time of the trial. Therefore, I hope that you are aware of this. You do know also that the Code which I have just cited, the Code of professional ethics, which is a basic document for us, states that the counsel, in paragraph 4 of the preamble, may be the subject of disciplinary measures provided in Article 47 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, of Rule 47, rather. This Rule 46, we don't want to get to that point either, and states that a Trial Chamber may, after a warning, refuse audience to counsel if in its opinion the conduct of that counsel is offensive, abusive or otherwise obstructs the proper conduct of the proceedings. This is the status of the question. There is not an immediate conflict, because as Judge Robinson said, we have yet gotten into the facts. But there is a potential conflict which is for sure -- even this is being challenged because it is none the less true that you were a participating party in some of the events. Therefore, I would like to ask whether you are aware of this, aware of the interests of the accused, and if you do not believe that it would be time to take the initiative yourself to disqualify yourself in order to avoid a real conflict of interest and this, of course, is in the interests of the proper conduct of the proceedings and the interests of justice. Thank very much. I would like you to answer my questions please and to my proposal as well, because I am making a proposal to you. I'm asking you to take the initiative yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you Your Honour, and for your remarks and warnings which I have understood fully. However, I cannot accept the position that I am a participant in certain events in which I happened to participate, by chance so to speak. I would accept that if that fact was disputed. However, that fact is not disputed, nor has the truthfulness of that fact been called in question by the statement of the accused or the statements of witnesses already heard. I'm fully conscious of the fact, and that is something that I have already said, that if I were to realise that there was a conflict of interest and that my participation could harm the interests of my client, I would withdraw myself, but bearing in mind the reasons the Prosecution is referring to, Mr. Tihic, Mr. Nalic, Mr. Bicic and Misic, I see absolutely no disputed fact. I have studied the motions carefully, I have studied the statements of the accused, I have studied the statements of other witnesses and victims and the other documents that have been disclosed to me, and nowhere have I seen any reason why I should appear as a witness. That is my position, and that is the reason why I will not take any more of your time. I will bear this in mind all the time. Should such a case occur, such a situation occur, I will reconsider, but for the moment I propose that this motion be rejected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Pisarevic [no interpretation]. Do you think that you could be called as a witness at some point in this trial either by the Prosecutor or by the accused, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) By Defence counsel I will not be called. I see no reason why the Prosecution would call me either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could you be called by -- called as a witness by other accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You mean in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, I don't think they will call me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could we have the representative for the Prosecutor again, please, Ms. MacFadyen. You heard the question that I asked in respect of Article 16. Do you think that Mr. Pisarevic might be called as a witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe in fact as I have indicated before my previous arguments that in fact at this point no one can indicate that they intend to call Mr. Pisarevic as a witness. However, I can see a likelihood, especially from what Mr. Pisarevic has described regarding his knowledge of these events, that he will be a necessary witness with respect to some events. For instance, the Omer Nalic event, where indeed he signed a power of attorney with respect to Omer Nalic, who will testify, and this goes to his credibility, that he was forced to sign a confession by Mr. Zaric. Mr. Pisarevic has indicated that he did not appear for Mr. Nalic, and yet there is a power of attorney signed. So there is an issue before the Court as to what he saw, whether he ever saw this confession or whether he didn't. I would suggest that that issue goes to the credibility of Mr. Nalic and everything that he will say as a witness. Also the fact that Mr. Pisarevic has indicated that he does not recognise any possibility for him being called as a witness either direct, or cross-examination, or as a rebuttal witness indicates that he does not understand the conflict. The conflict is simply that he has personal knowledge of disputed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Pisarevic, have you got anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All I can say additionally is that all the points made by the Prosecution have no bearing on these proceedings, whether and why I went to see Mr. Nalic, this is not a subject of trial. This matter can be investigated when I'm brought to trial, but this fact has nothing to do with the case that I am participating in as Defence counsel. All these allegations are mere insinuations, and the aim is to eliminate me from the Defence because I'm a person who lived there, who, it is true, is quite familiar with those people there, the people know him, I am aware of the conditions under which the people are living there, which is quite normal. I spend the whole period there. Maybe the aim of the Prosecution is to eliminate all the attorneys who were in that area in Republika Srpska and who participated in a sense in that armed conflict, but I think that better assistance and more qualified defence cannot be provided to these accused than by the people who were there present, of course, with the assistance of other colleagues. I really think that there is no conflict of interest, but I suggest that you hear perhaps my client and the other accused on the matter, and if you consider it proper then you make the decision to eliminate me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We have heard in detail full this whole question of the conflict of interest through the submissions and through the presentations this morning. I have told you of the Trial Chamber's concerns. I have given you an oral warning. The Trial Chamber will take the time to deliberate the issue. You will do so in writing, and if necessary, you will also ask that the accused take a position himself, or themselves. It is now 11.30, almost 11.30. We're going to suspend the hearing to allow the interpreters, whom I would like to thank, by the way, for their co-operation. We're going to take a half hour break as we ordinarily do, and the Trial Chamber will resume at noon, in the order that I've already announced, that is the motion on judicial notice of the character of the conflict and then judicial notice of adjudicated facts. This will be done after the break, that is at noon. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12:00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) As I said at the end of the first part of the morning's work, we're resuming the hearing, and I will give the floor immediately to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor to speak to us about their position on judicial notice of the international character of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina and on established facts. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just make one brief statement before I begin my argument, as you will notice, I have switched places with my colleague because the physical arrangement of this courtroom makes it extremely difficult for the person sitting in this chair to see both Judge Robinson and to see Mr. Zaric, one of the defendants, because the view is blocked by the column. I asked the Court officers if they could move Mr. Zaric to the other seat there so that he and I could see each other, and I was informed that they could not, for security reasons. So that I could see Your Honours and Mr. Zaric, I have moved to this location. And if there is any possibility in the future to setting up the courtroom in a somewhat different physical manner, it would be of great assistance to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, taking in mind your admonitions to keep our comments brief and to attempt not to repeat anything in our written submissions, I will attempt as best as possible to do that. And as you noted, it is possible to essentially argue both of our motions concerning adjudicated facts together, so I will attempt as much as possible to combine my two arguments. In our motion concerning the judicial notice of the international nature of the armed conflict, what we have asked to court to do is take judicial notice of the fact that between the 6th of March 1992 and the 19th of May, 1992, it has been determined by this Court and it is a historical fact of common knowledge that the nature of the conflict during that period was one of an international nature. There was an international conflict at least until the 19th of May. It is the position of the prosecutors's office that there was an international conflict throughout the entire war in Bosnia and the rest of the former Yugoslavia. However, we concede that the period after the 19th of May is more complicated and is in dispute in other cases before this Tribunal. Therefore we have tried to be reasonable and ask the Court to simply focus on that period between the 6th of March and the 19th of May, when we contend it is not in dispute that it was an international armed conflict. As Your Honours know, under Rule 94 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Court has the authority to take judicial notice. There are two provisions, two subrules to that: There is subrule "A", which deals with facts of common knowledge, and there's subrule "B", which deals with adjudicated facts from other proceedings before the Tribunal. It's our contention that Your Honours can find this to be an adjudicated fact -- that you can take judicial notice of this under either of those provisions. You can either find that this is a historical fact of common knowledge, or in the alternative, you could rule that this is an adjudicated fact that has already been determined in other proceedings before the Tribunal. We would note that the theory behind judicial notice is that of judicial economy as a way to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: We would note that the theory behind judicial notice is one of judicial economy; that one of the purposes for the rule is to expedite the proceedings so that the Court does not have to hear evidence of facts of common knowledge or facts that have already been determined by another court of law. We would note that if we are forced to produce evidence concerning the international nature of the conflict, it would require calling a large number of witnesses, a number of experts and that in essence this Court would hear evidence which it has already heard in previous cases, and may hear multiple times during to course of the Tribunal. We would note that the Defence itself concedes in their response to our motion that the concept of judicial notice is useful to expedite the hearing of a case and to produce uniformity of decisions in certain matters. There can perhaps be no more important matter before this Tribunal than determining the nature of the conflict, since this is an international Tribunal created by an international agency the United Nations, which was designed to deal with an international conflict. Therefore we think that this is a particularly significant fact that must be determined once and for all by this Court. We would also note that part of the reason we have brought this notion at that time is in response to encouragement that was given to us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefits of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I would attempt to slow down Your Honour as I have been instructed, I would ask the interpreters to appreciate that I need to make my arguments in my own fashion. So, I will do the best I can. I would note that in an earlier Status Conference Judge Rodrigues encouraged us to take advantage of all the different provisions in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as a means of expediting the trial. I think we are all in agreement that the trials before this Tribunal have taken a long period of time. We are all of the opinion that it would be in the best interests of all the parties to try and expedite these cases and we feel that this is a means for doing so. Getting down to our arguments concerning whether this is a fact of common knowledge or an adjudicated fact, we would contend that the international nature of the conflicts is clearly a historical fact that is no longer open to dispute. As I stated earlier we must remember the special mandate of the Tribunal. We are an international Tribunal established by an international organisation to resolve an international conflicts. The limited jurisdiction that this Tribunal has means that by necessity, all of the cases coming before it will deal exclusively with the facts related to the war in the former Yugoslavia. And in every single case facts and evidence will have to be presented about the nature of the conflict, unless the Court takes judicial notice. We believe that the fact that this was an international conflict is a historical fact, much as it can be stated that, for example, there was a war fought by the United States in Vietnam in the 1960s and 70s. That's a fact that's no longer in historical dispute, everyone agrees that that happened and we would contend that that is the type of fact that could be seen as a fact of common knowledge. We could say that thousands of people unfortunately died here in Holland during World War II. I think that is a fact that would be agreed as a fact of common knowledge, requires no further proof. Like those historical facts we contend that the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence on the 6th of March, 1992, is a fact that is no longer in dispute, that's a historical fact. And we also condenied that the fact that there was an armed conflict going on in Bosnia in which the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army, which was the army of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, another country, was involved in that war. We believe those facts together show that this was an international conflict. If Your Honours are not willing to see this as a historical fact that you can take notice of as a fact of common knowledge, we would argue that you can take notice of this because it's an adjudicated fact that has already been adjudicated before other proceedings of the Tribunal. As Your Honours are aware, the Tadic case and the Celebici case have beenconcluded; they have rendered their verdicts. And while we acknowledge that both of those cases are on appeal, it is our contention that this fact is one that is not being appealed, and therefore any decisions that have been made by those courts are final decisions as to this particular fact, making it an adjudicated fact. I would just remind you that the both the Tadic and Celebici cases in their written decisions have found that at least from the period of the 6th of March, 1992, until the 19th of May, 1992, this was an international conflict. In the decision on the Defence motion for interlocutory appeal in the Tadic case, the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has also found that that was an international conflict, citing both the date of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the involvement of the Yugoslav National Army. In both the final opinions and judgements in the Tadic case and the Celebici cases, they too stated that they had found that at least from the 6th of March 1992 until the 19th of May, there was an international conflict ongoing in Bosnia. And finally, the Appeals Chamber in the Defence motion for interlocutory appeal in the Tadic case also found that the conflict was international in nature, at least until the 19th of May, 1992. We have also noted that similar decisions were reached in the Rule 61 hearings before this Tribunal. Now, we acknowledge that Rule 61 proceedings are not full-blown trials and that an argument could be made that those facts are not adjudicated facts. That being said, however, we do think that the decisions of those Rule 61 courts can nonetheless be looked at as corroborating evidence, as further evidence that there is a unanimous consensus among the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal that this fact is in fact a determined, undisputable fact. I would note, in the decision of the Karadzic/Mladic Rule 61 hearing, it was stated that the Trial Chamber considers that at the time it began in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the present conflict was international in character insofar as it involved two distinct states, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the SFRY, later the FRY. As we noted in our written motion, three different foreign courts have also come to the same conclusion, that this was an international conflict. Two courts in Germany and a military tribunal in Switzerland have found that during the period of time we are asking, from March until May, that it was an international conflict. And finally I would note that Judge May, who unfortunately is not present today himself, has taken judicial notice of the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence from the Socialist Federated Republic of Yugoslavia on the 3rd of March, 1992, and that was in the Kovacevic decision of 12 May, 1998. And further, Judge May took judicial notice of the fact that the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state was recognised by the European commission on 6 April 1992, and by the United States on 7 April 1992. Having recognised the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was one of the most important points in establishing the international nature of the conflict. As I said, the Defence has made several arguments against the Court finding this to be an adjudicated fact. But I would simply note that we take some exception to the argument made by the Defence citing that we should be using rule 73 bis instead of Rule 94, adjudicated facts, to deal with issues of this sort. Rule 73 bis deals with the Pre-Trial conference in which the parties are asked to submit agreed-upon facts and facts in matters that are not in dispute. While we certainly intend to fully use that option, and will submit to the Court many facts that we hope the Defence will stipulate to, I must note that Mr. Pantelic stated to us on an earlier occasion that the only thing he would stipulate to was his client's date of birth. And it was partly because of that statement that we did not have much confidence that we could approach the Defence and work out an agreement ahead of time concerning this matter. I would just note that as has been ruled in the previous decisions I've cited to, it's important to look to the definition of an international conflict, the Geneva Conventions. The Geneva Conventions in Article 2 explains what they consider to be the definition of international conflict, and I will not repeat that for you; I'm sure you've read that in our motion. The ICRC commentary also takes a very broad view of the definition of international armed conflict, and I would note that that ICRC commentary has been cited by both the Tadic and Celebici chambers in their decisions on the matter. I would also like to note that the Swiss government has also back-dated the accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Geneva Conventions to 6 March 1992: Again, more evidence that that is a significant date at the point at which an international conflict can be concluded. It's our contention that the character of the conflict being that it was international between March and May 1992 is indisputable. We contend that the Defence would not be able to come before this Court and present any evidence to the contrary. We believe that it is in the interests of judicial economy to find this fact now, so that we do not have to present a large number of witnesses and an extraordinary amount of documentary evidence, evidence that this chamber may not have itself heard but certainly other chambers have heard, and would have to be repeated over and over and over again in the future in all trials before the Tribunal if it is not decided at this point in time. So it's our contention that fact of the international nature of the conflict is indisputable and should be judicially noticed either as a fact of common knowledge or as an adjudicated fact. As to our second motion, concerning the list of 170 facts which we have asked the Court to take judicial notice of, we believe that the same arguments can be made: That the Court can take judicial notice under either 94(A), that these are facts of common knowledge, we would contend that all of them can be classified as historical facts, or we would argue that you can also find that these are adjudicated facts that have been previously determined by other chambers in the Tribunal. Every one of the facts that we have listed in that list of 170 facts we have taken from the written decisions of the Tadic and the Celebici cases. Both of those cases have come to verdict, and final decisions have been issued. Again I would acknowledge that both of those cases are on appeal, but it's our contention that the facts that we are asking you to notice are not being appealed; they are not the source of the appeal. Therefore, as to them, the decision is final, and they can be seen as adjudicated facts. I will not again repeat the arguments I have just made concerning the powers to take judicial notice. I would just like to, in addressing those particular facts, move the Court's attention specifically to facts 159 to 170 in our motion. Those are the ones that deal with an armed conflict. As I have just argued, we believe that there is irrefutable evidence that there was an international armed conflict ongoing in Bosnia and Herzegovina from at least March to May 1992, and therefore it follows that we also contend that there was an armed conflict, whether or not it was international or internal in character. Again I would note that not only the Tadic and Celebici chambers have found that to be true, but in the Furundzija case, which has also gone to verdict, they have found that there was an armed conflict ongoing in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the time periods that we are asking the Court to take judicial notice. As with the nature of the international conflict, we contend that this fact is irrefutable, that the Defence cannot bring any evidence before this Court that will change that determination. And we would ask the Court specifically to take judicial notice of those facts of armed conflict. We would go on, however, to point out that all of the rest of the facts, numbers 1 to 158 listed in our annex, we contend, are also either facts of common knowledge -- by that I would mean historical facts which courts can ordinarily take notice of -- or we would contend that they are adjudicated facts, since every one of them has been addressed in written decisions and findings of at least two, if not three, of the chambers before this Tribunal. We believe that that constitutes adjudicated facts. So it's for those reasons, Your Honours, that we have brought these motions before the Court today. We feel that it is clearly in the interests of judicial economy to resolve these matters now, not only to save the time of the Court, but so that we can make a determination of what witnesses we need to call and what evidence we need to present. If the Court were to judicially notice these facts, it would greatly shorten the length of the trial, and we believe would serve not only the interests of the Prosecution by the interests of the Defence as well. We would ask that Your Honours take acknowledgement of the fact that has been already mentioned by me on a couple of occasions, that being it is indisputable that on the 6th of March, 1992, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence; it was internationally recognised in April of 1992. There is no dispute before the chambers of this Tribunal that the JNA, the military army of another country, was involved in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if this Court looks to the definition under the Geneva Conventions, it will see that that meets the definition of international armed conflict. And we would respectfully ask this Court to take notice of that fact, as well as the 170 other facts that we have presented in our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. Paterson. I note that for the Defence, there was a response which I have before me, which was presented by Defence counsel, Mr. Abramovic for Mr. Simic, Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Saint Just for Mr. Tadic, Mr. Brashic for Mr. Todorvic, and Mr. Pisarevic for Mr. Zaric. Who is going to speak on behalf of the Defence in this hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: (No interpretation).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Very briefly, with regard to general issues, I will, and I believe that my brother, Mr. Pantelic, will address specific issues. The Court is being asked to interpret certain decisions of other Trial Chambers that between the period of March 6, 1992, and May 19, 1992, there existed an international conflict on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The concept of an adjudicated fact is one where the Court has rendered a decision, and it can be broken down, at least in Anglo-Saxon jurisprudence, as one of either collateral estoppel or res judicata. We have the Tadic and we have the Celebici decisions. They were made by other Trial Chambers. These defendants were not party to those proceedings. These defence attorneys did not proffer witnesses, documents, or most importantly, interpretations of certain facts. The Prosecutor, as an example, states that there was a Vietnamese war. Well, being somewhat of a historian, there was a conflict in Viet Nam. People got killed. Napalm was used. Bombing of Laos and Cambodia took place. Was it a war as defined by the United States constitution? No. So it is this specific issue of how you interpret historical facts, that people were shooting in Bosnia and Herzegovina; that the JNA, until March, was on its own territory, and poof, by a piece of paper, a purely local civil conflict, strife, is changed into a different animal, with different repercussions, different penalties, different rules. Now, I was not counsel in the Celebici case. I was not counsel in the Tadic case. I do not know what was in the mind of Defence counsel there. I do not know what was in the mind of the Trial Chamber. You are an independent body, and you are an independent finder of fact. I have a situation in the United States District Court for the Southern District where across one hallway, Judge Kaplan found a fact to be totally different and have different applications than Judge Koeltl across the hall, again dealing with the disintegration of Yugoslavia. Judge Koeltl has found that it was not a political issue that was before him. Judge Kaplan found that it was a political issue before him, and dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction. I think that the Defence has the right and the obligation to independently have its own witnesses, its own experts, interpret historical occurrences. I must concur with Ms. Paterson with regard to the other issue: The 168 -- at least that was in my motion papers -- 168 facts. A lot of them are nondisputable. However, the further we come to the present, the further interpretations are necessary. That the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was established in 1919, granted. That in 1929 that Kingdom changed its name to Yugoslavia, granted. When we get to the tail-end, the 158 to 168, at least in the copy that I received by telefax, that is subject to interpretation, and that is not a matter that Defence can concede, as the earlier determinations by other Chambers in which we were not parties cannot be collateral estoppel to us or res judicata. Final sentence: The concept of judicial notice is that 1 pound one equals 2.2 kilograms, that speed of light is, if memory serves me, some 360 odd thousand miles per either second or minute. Those are facts that the Court can take. The minute you have interpretation, you need live witnesses, experts to guide the Court and to make an independent determined decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- I understand you to be saying that judicial notice, certainly in the Anglo Saxon system, is built on collateral estoppel and the concept of res judicata, and you seem to be saying for that reason your client has a right to an independent determination of all issues of fact, but have you addressed specifically Rule 94(B), which deals with a particular species of judicial notice, and in that provision judicial notice is, it seems to me, a term of art. It is setting up its own peculiar system as to what it is that the Trial Chamber may take judicial notice of, and it says that the Chamber may take judicial notice of adjudicated facts from other proceedings of the Tribunal relating to matters at issue in the current proceedings. Is it your contention that in a situation where that would ordinarily be applicable, that there is still this right to an independent determination of the facts at issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am still wrestling with the Rules. I used to teach trial practice and procedure, but these Rules are new to me. I think the only way I can answer, Your Honour, is that both the Prosecutor and I view this as a duality of issue. We have the issue of adjudicated facts, and then we have the issue of common knowledge. The common knowledge is what I described in the later part of my argument as being judicial notice of the fact that a pound is 2.2 kilograms. With regard to Your Honour's question as to adjudicated fact, Rule 94(B) speaks about the ability of the Court to extract from other decisions certain facts which are not in question and to make them and adopt them. My argument to Your Honour is that both the Celebici case and the Tadic case, if this Trial Chamber was sitting as a District Court in New York, the decision in the Tadic case and the Celebici case by some Judge across the hall or downstairs would not be binding on the United States District Court Judge. It would be advisory only, and no further deference should be given to a decision of a Trial Chamber of equal stature as this Chamber. That is why I brought up the concept that Judge Kaplan on floor 12 in the District Court, and Judge Koeltl across the hall on floor 12 of the District Court have two different opinions. I think that this Court, as an independent body, is charged with making its own independent determinations as to interpretations of fact, especially in the light of the -- I'm now being redundant in using "fact" too many times, especially due to the fact, again, that we were not party to those proceedings. We did not have any input as to who the Defence called, what theories they advanced or who the Prosecution might have called in that case and who they may call in this case. So as an independent attorney in this case, I urge the Court that it has to make, as to the crucial issues with regard to the international nature of the conflict of that period, its own independent determination should it want to grant and afford the Defence a proper hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, just one or two other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand your analysis to be applicable to the situation where the facts of which judicial notice is being taken, derived from a decision of a court or a Chamber of coordinate jurisdiction. I think you said the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you have the same view if the facts of which judicial notice are being taken come from a decision of the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In the United States, Your Honour, totally different position with regard to a decision in the -- in this International Criminal Tribunal, I do not know that answer, Your Honour. I would, if I had to argue, I would -- based on my concept of law and jurisprudence, I think if the Appeals Chamber had resolved the issue, I think it would be binding upon you, sitting as a Trial Chamber Judge, but that is an opinion, that is my wish that the concept of law in which I work would be applicable to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Brashich. Thank you. Having reminded us this is an International Tribunal, in fact, and that, therefore, we take into account what takes place in this or that legal system, but we only take notice of that. We are an International Tribunal. Thank you for having recalled the practice in the United States, but not -- there is not only the United States, there are other countries. This is an International Tribunal. We take note of what takes place in various places and the general principles of International Law which guide us in the last analysis, of course. I will now give the floor, as you suggested, to Mr. Pantelic to speak on behalf of the Defence about the two motions, that is the international character of the conflict and adjudicated facts, that is the two motions that are being discussed right now. Mr. Pantelic, you may proceed. Please co-operate with us in respect of the time, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Our idea, three Defence counsels in this case, is to submit some very general issues from two major legal systems, Common Law and Civil Law. In our internal agreements, we came to the conclusion that it would be fully in accordance with the judicial economy, and with the principles of submissions of the parties in this case that my learned colleague, Mr. Brashich, as he already gave his very good and fundamental overview of Common Law system, then I would suggest that my learned colleague from France, lawyer Saint Just, will have the floor for maximum few minutes, five minutes or ten minutes, with regard to the Civil Law issues, general issues in general terms which may be applicable to the practice of ICTY. And then with your permission, I would make a few short and precise references to some of the issues raised by the OTP, the Prosecutor, and of course, related to our motions. So in total, I think that we shall spend not more than 15 or 20 minutes, having in mind that very important issue which we are discussing now, various angle of view. I kindly ask for your attention at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If I've understood you correctly, Mr. Pantelic, you are suggesting that, first, Mr. Saint Just take the floor for a maximum of five minutes and then who would speak directly afterwards, you yourself--

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) -- for about ten minutes. All right. Mr. Saint Just is going to speak for five minutes and then you will follow for ten minutes. Is that it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, please understand. Well, it's true the question is important, but we also have to take into account the needs of time, and remember that we have the written submissions before us. Let me remind you that we have these submissions in writing and that we've read them carefully, and, therefore, for judicial economy I ask that you not repeat what is already presented in writing. Mr. Saint Just, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour, I will be brief, but you know the beneficial virtues of a public hearing with both parties present. Of course, this is an extremely important case, extremely important question, and we have to look at the efforts made by the Prosecutor in order to come to a favourable decision. There are two or three points that struck me in the Prosecutor's comments. First of all, it was her will to achieve expeditiousness and judicial economy, and I agree that justice may be expeditious but we must not confuse haste and speed, and in all cases the parties must be allowed to prepare a full defence. The Prosecutor almost threw a challenge at us by saying that she was sure that were the Defence to have the chance to have the opportunity to plead as to the international character the Defence could not prove anything further. This was a kind of challenge which you've thrown at us, and you want to tie our hands and our feet by saying that I'm sure you will be able to prove anything and that you would not have the right to prove anything because we're going to refer this to judicial notice. But I, Your Honour, do not at all consider that. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you have the right to make that judicial notice pursuant to Rules 94(A) and (B), but I don't think you can do it in this case. Why do I say that? What you are being asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You're talking about the international character of the conflict, of the first motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAINT JUST
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, the first motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Not the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Not the second what we're asking is to accept the international character of the conflict. That it's doing so is not only accepting certain facts but to accepting the legal conclusion drawn from those facts. You can very well have -- make judicial notice of certain facts in respect of judicial economy and speed. You can refer to testimonies of witnesses or to documents that were given in other cases, that would be possible, but in respect of the legal consequences of the interpretation and review of all the testimony, and all the arguments and all the documents in respect of the international character, you cannot make a judicial -- take judicial notice. What would that mean? It would mean that you are prohibiting the Defence today, the defence of these accused and these counsel who are here today, prohibiting them from bringing in new testimony, new arguments, new facts and new evaluations, and I believe that this is completely unacceptable. You can apply the Rule, but when it deals with facts in the way we've just described and the facts that the Prosecutor has raised, that's possible. It's certainly not in respect of the international character of the conflict itself. In that respect you must give your opinion, your own opinion, you, a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, in respect of the international character, after having allowed, of course, the Defence to discuss and to make -- and to bring in all of these elements in respect to its own interpretation. I believe that acting in that way would be taking into account -- I'm not asking that you make -- take judicial notice of Roman Law or Civil Law, but to take into account all these Rules, because you have certainly, Your Honour, seen that in the response from Mr. Pantelic, which was -- includes the work in things that I did, having to do with judicial notice in my country of France. I'm not going to repeat it today. This was presented in writing. But of course, you saw that in France this is an extremely significant issue, a very exciting one which goes back to the quarrels of the Acien regime, which is still relevant today, and that case law and authors have always expressed themselves extremely firmly on this subject, and have said that in France, judging through judicial notice, which was called the reference method, that -- which is prohibited by the Civil Code, and was also prohibited by the constitutions of the French Revolution because these were violations of the fundamental principles of law, and violations of the principle of having both parties present, and violations of an equitable trial which is recognising that all international documents, including the New York covenant, et cetera, et cetera, but, in fact, it would be a -- it would be a miscarriage of justice. This is what I believe. There are certain facts, very simple ones, which cannot be challenged, and of those you can take judicial notice, but in respect of other facts having -- coming to -- having to do with coming to the conclusion as to the existence of an international character in this conflict, you can only allow the defence to have the right to discuss this issue. The Defence will not delay the trial, will not be obstructionist, it will do its work, and you cannot prevent it from carrying out its rights and to obtaining its rights and, I think, doing the -- anything else, and this, in fact, is where we reach a very crucial question in this case.
