This is something which you must really allow us to do, that is to discuss this question of law. Lastly, I will conclude by saying, Your Honour, briefly, that in respect of the second motion of the Prosecution having to do with this case and with the question which you asked my colleague, I personally believe that even if the Appeals Chamber were to take a position in respect of the facts or legal consequences requested by the Prosecutor, you, as an independent Trial Chamber, would not be obligated to take that into account, that in your judgement you could not say that considering that the Appeals Court in other case ruled that we, the Trial Chamber, must, therefore, rule in that way. You could refer to it, of course, because this would be an Appeals Chamber, but you would have no obligation, in fact, to follow what they have said, and that's what I believe firmly. What the Prosecutor is asking you, and I'm almost finished, since we are talking about ruling about the international conflict -- character of the conflict, in fact, this is taking away your freedom as a Trial Chamber and in a sense not respecting your own functioning, the grandeur and august nature of your function. Remember that you are an International Tribunal, something which has not been seen very frequently before. In fact, the entire world is watching you and your responsibility is very great. And to say in your judgement that this issue of law was already adjudicated, therefore we're not going to re-judge it, I think that would be asking you to limit your freedom completely and not to consider yourself as a real court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Saint Just, I would like to note something that you referred to Rule 94, which has to do with the jurisdiction of the Trial Chamber and say that you have to make a distinction between the existence of a fact and the legal conclusion to be drawn from that fact. I note that there are facts and, in fact, we will see -- we will consider this issue very seriously in our -- from the depths of our conscience, and there is the interpretation and the legal conclusion that should be drawn from these facts. I will note this distinction you have made. Judge Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saint Just, in your submissions, I understood you to be saying that this Trial Chamber would not necessarily be bound to take judicial notice of a fact that has been adjudicated by the Appeals Chamber. If that is so, are you then saying that Rule 94(B) has no scope of application, because what would be the scope of application for Rule 94(B) if the Trial Chamber cannot exercise the discretion which is given to it under 94(B) to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts not from another Trial Chamber but from the Appeals Chamber. I can understand the argument in relation to another Trial Chamber which is a Chamber of coordinate jurisdiction, but what then would be the scope of application for 94(B) if the Trial Chamber is not allowed to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts from other proceedings of the Appeals Chamber? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: Regarding the Appeals Chamber judgement, today we know that the two decisions referred to have still not been resolved by the Appeals Chamber, therefore your argument doesn't hold. As for the effect of a decision of an Appeals Chamber, it is quite certain that if an Appeals Chamber, there is no cassation Court here but the Appeals Chamber being the final chamber, I think that you have to bear it in mind, but I still consider that regarding the interpretation and the legal consequences, it is still up to you, that is the Trial Chamber, you still have complete freedom to judge in one way or another. In other words, Your Honours, I do not think that in your decision, you can be satisfied by saying that the Appeals Chamber has ruled in such-and-such a way. Of course you can refer to it as one of your arguments, but I think you're obliged to motivate yourself any legal decision that you take yourself, and to provide the motivation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. We are not here to judge relationships between the Chamber and the Appeals Chamber. We have the statute, and if an Appeals Chamber decides to revise a decision or to send it back to the Trial Chamber, they have to do accordingly. An Appeals Chamber is obliged to harmonise the jurisprudence, and it goes without saying that we have to take into account, but we are not obliged textually to be bound by its decisions. And this is something specific to this International Tribunal. I now give the floor to Mr. Pantelic, who is going to intervene as the last speaker this morning on behalf of the Defence, therefore for about ten minutes, to conclude the response of the Defence regarding judicial notice and regarding the international conflict and the established facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After the very profound and professional submissions of my learned colleague, I could just take this possibility to have a short overview of the mutual motions and response to the motions and some other theoretical questions about the judicial notice, collateral estoppel, res judicata, and general terms which should be our guideline here in the Tribunal; that's fairness of trial. First of all, I have to note that the former members of the Prosecutor bench, namely Justice Richard Goldstone, former Prosecutor of ICTY, in his submissions, the interlocutory appeal hearings for the Tadic case a few years before, made some references to very distinguished and learned colleague, His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, who at the same time made other references to words of Sir -- I think it's Judge Patrick Fitzmorris. So all persons in question stated unanimously that use of doctrine of judicial notice, in no matter which legal system, but especially in the proceedings before international courts -- and this Court is without a doubt, it's a fact of common knowledge, is an international Court -- so the use of this doctrine should be very conservative. Because in proceedings before International Court of Justice where the parties are governments, states, that's another problem. But here, where the person is -- individual is in question, there is no government, there is nobody to cover him, to help him. And the role of the Court is, according to the Rules, is to respect his right for defence. So in conclusion, use of judicial notice, especially before ICTY and during our proceedings, should be absolutely restrictive and conservative. In our written motion -- I mean response to motion, to these motions, we attached hundreds of pages of various theoretical issues, more than 400 pages, about the practice in the United States, Canada, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Australia -- I mean, mainly in common law systems as well as civil law. I don't want to make any particular reference to that; everything is there. His Honour Judge Robinson made, from my point of view, very important reference to one issue on which I would like to give some comments. The fact is that if, for example, in Tadic or Celebici judgement, Appeals Chamber will practically serve the same in general terms, judgement in relation to the nature of conflict, the question is: Is this decision or particular Trial Chamber should be bound by this decision? My personal position is in favour of this approach, but I have some reserves to that, very factual. Speaking about the Tadic proceedings, his Defence counsel, a Dutchman, distinguished colleague, Mr. Vladimirov, was not interested at all about these general issues and questions. He stated that many times. I know because I have some personal relations. In Tadic case, furthermore --in Celebici case; sorry -- the Defence for the accused person consisted of Croat and Muslim lawyers, including some other colleagues from Canada, the States, et cetera. But the very issue about the nature of conflict was also not so important for this particular case. This case, Samac case, in chronology of proceedings before ICTY, is the first case where the Defence is in position to serve and to submit some documents which were not at all hypothetically even possible to be in possession of either Defence counsels in other cases about this very precise and very important issue, the nature of conflict. Namely, about the involvement -- alleged involvement -- of JNA, Yugoslav army, in operations in Bosnia. Now, we are facing one procedural situation here. I think that -- and my interpretation of Rule 94, subrule B, the words which I would like to refer are "after hearing the parties, may decide to take judicial notice." What does it mean, "after hearing the parties"? It's not a simple situation that we shall submit our arguments, the other party will hear it, Trial Chamber will decide; no. In this -- well, that's my interpretation; that's my approach. In this particular situation, we have to have special hearing about the fundamental issues, if one party will ask for it. And I will tell you why we should hear, in terms of judicial economy, have this special hearing. Personally that would be injustice for me, and my colleagues in this case, to be bound by the conclusions of Appeal Chamber about the nature of conflicts, because how someone can speak about the nature of conflict without the presence of very important evidence, documentation, at least one party in question, and one party in question is former Yugoslavia People's Army, JNA, do you think that learned colleague from Holland and learned colleagues from Bosnia and from Croatia could even think about the possibility to take some other very, very confidential documents from the archives of the headquarters of JNA, and then put it before one Trial Chamber and discuss about the possible nature of the conflict? So we have to be very, very conservative about this very nature, this moment. Because we didn't see that before in other cases. Theoretically, you can say "well, we have now a final decision in Tadic and Celebici cases; we have to be bound by this general issue." But Your Honour, just a second, please, I just come to my point, please. So we could say theoretically yes -- my suggestion in terms of judicial economy, Your Honour, that's my conclusion, is -- and this is a short reference to some submissions of my learned colleague, Ms. Paterson, I firmly believe that if you are speaking about the Pre-Trial conferences in terms of rule 73 bis, it is not the means that we have to have one date and one special hearing for all these things. Pre-Trial period is a large period, I mean that's not the question of day, that's a period. And I strongly suggest this Trial Chamber to grant our proposal to have special hearing with not more than two or three expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Pantelic, allow me to interrupt you. I'm interrupting you to tell you the following: This is an approach that I do not share, because you are referring to another problem. The question that we are addressing is the following: Judicial notice. We are not going to redo the Tadic or the Celebici trials. We are proceeding on the basis of a motion submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor regarding the international character of the conflict from such-and-such a date until such-and-such a date. You have expressed your standpoint in writing; if you have additional elements to contribute, this is the occasion to do so. Secondly, regarding a certain number of facts mentioned in another motion with appropriate numbers that have been discussed a moment ago, clearly they go up to 168. To hear the parties, that is not to present evidence all over again. It is only to see whether we can take judicial notice or not, and for what reasons. That is all. Therefore I disagree with you. We are not going to have another hearing on these questions with expert witnesses; that is not the problem. That is not the question we are addressing; I'm sorry to tell you that. You're outside the scope of the issue. The issue is there is a motion, there is response of the Defence that we have read, I have taken note of the comments by Mr. Saint Just regarding the facts and the interpretation of facts and the legal consequences of those facts; I have taken note of his position. If you have supplementary elements to contribute to that question, the Trial Chamber is ready to give you a few more minutes, after which we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Everything is in connection with this issue. I would say, as I stated in my written submissions, I said that there is no legal possibility to take judicial notice about the term which is not a fact. Speaking about the fact of independence of Bosnia, we cannot say that that's a fact, because for one state to be independent in the international public law terms, there are some preconditions, and very easily we could challenge that. I will now just bring your attention on another fact which is very important, and finally we will see why these facts are important for the interests of the individual, my client. Because after that, if we take without any critical approach this fact, we could say well that's a fact, 6th of March,'92, Bosnia was recognised as an independent state. Ergo, JNA was there, ergo international conflicts, ergo my client is in a problem because application of Geneva Conventions under this factual situation is completely different than if you are speaking about civil war, and speaking about the nature. So therefore I think it's premature to open all these questions and to speak about all this. And just give my opinion that we should need at least to hear, I would say theoretically third party, all these proceedings. We heard Croats, Muslims, finally lets hear Serbs. Why not? About this very important issue. I just stated why. So by nature, judicial notice in this particular case cannot be taken about the nature of conflict, because it's a theoretical -- it's not fact; it's a theoretical question, requesting very profound expertise, which we don't see at the moment. In spite of some findings in Tadic and Celebici case, controversial, absolutely unfounded, a big error in law. So if you need, Your Honour, some other submission about the second motion, I can proceed, or maybe I can do that after, about the second motion 40(P), concerning the list of facts and the nature of these facts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am going to adjourn, because of the good cooperation of the interpreters, whom I thank in passing. We will resume at 2.30 sharp. We have heard you on the nature of the conflict as well as your co-counsel, Mr. Saint Just; we also heard Mr. Brassic. I think that the arguments of the Defence have been amply developed regarding the international character of the conflicts. I will give the floor again when we resume work regarding the second motion, that is taking judicial notice on adjudicated facts. Mr. Brassic, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour I am under order by Judge Turner of the United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee to be available by telephone at 3.00 for approximately five minutes. I was wondering if I could at 3.00, if I could ask for a recess to take the call as to scheduling of a case in Tennessee where I represent the defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is very difficult for me to adjourn the hearing for -- you said five minutes? Five minutes? I won't adjourn the hearing, because you have a telephone appointment. However, if you wish to leave the hall for five minutes, you will ask permission of the Court. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We can now resume the hearing at the point where we left off this morning. I give the floor to Mr. Pantelic, who should speak about the issue of adjudicated facts and judicial notice. That is our motion -- or another motion, rather, because the Defence had already spoken about the first motion having to do with the international character of the conflict. Mr. Pantelic, you may proceed. I request, given the -- the magnitude of our work today, to keep the time in mind when you present your arguments, because many of the arguments have already been submitted in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will follow your instructions. First of all, before I start with my submissions in regard to the second motion, officially on behalf of all Defence counsels I would like to officially ask from the Court to take my oral motion, which is as follows: Defence respectfully ask for a special hearing about the issue of -- nature of the conflict, or if it's not granted, Defence would like to offer and propose an offer of proof as following -- the evidence as following, Defence would like to introduce in these particular proceedings the following evidences, an agreement by warring parties in BHA on May 22nd, '92 with the presence of ICRC members. Then strictly confidential internal documents from JNA headquarters in Belgrade relating to the retreat process in Bosnia in May '92, and other expert witness opinions related to the International Public Law issues, meaning of control of territory of Bosnia and then all other relations between March and 19 May, '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Just to clarify Mr. Pantelic's statement, what the Defence offers at this present time, should a request for an evidentiary hearing not be granted as to the issue in motion number one, for the record, we are making a formal offer of proof that should such a hearing have been held, we would have offered into evidence at that time an agreement between the parties in conflict under the auspices and sanctions of the International Committee for the Red Cross in May 1992, which specifically found as to the nature of the conflict at that time. We are further prepared to offer in evidence at such a hearing internal documents, beginning at least March 1992, showing that the JNA was an army in retreat, and that any actions taken by it were as a defensive measure and not as measures taken as acts of war. We would further offer at such a hearing, should it be granted, expert testimony as to the nature of the conflict. Should we have such a hearing, the Defence is prepared to offer into evidence facts which would show that the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at that time, was not controlled by a central authority and that 70 to 73 per cent of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich, I regret having to interrupt you. I've understood the motion, and I don't need any additional arguments. We are not now getting into the very essence of the subject, I've already said that this morning. I am sorry that you're insisting on that point. I believe that having told you that we must remain within the scope of the subject. This is not the trial. We are not now proving facts, nor are we producing evidence in respect of any facts. This is simply a Pre-Trial motion, and this motion requires judicial notice. I've understood the oral submission by Mr. Pantelic. I've just heard it. I'm going to consult with my colleague Judge Robinson for a few moments. Thank you. I will give the floor to the Office of the Prosecutor, its representative, in order to express her point of view on this oral motion which was just presented by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would oppose the request of the Defence, primarily because they have made this request not in a timely manner. They had sufficient opportunity up until the end of the day yesterday to file any motions or responses to our motions. I believe that in essence this is essentially what Mr. Brashich said in his response to our motion, that if he was requesting an order for a hearing on the facts, the motions submitted by the other three Defence focused more on the issue of judicial notice than the issue of such a hearing. Certainly they have been free to make these documents available to the Court. Obviously, it's up to the Court's discretion if, under the circumstances, you want to accept the documents. We have not seen the documents, I don't know what the documents are that they're referring to, so I'm not in a position to comment on their relevance. Our position is simply that it's not timely, and, as you point out, that's not really the issue here. The issue is whether or not you can take judicial notice. If you rule that you cannot or will not take judicial notice, then we proceed to trial and prove our case accordingly, and they will have sufficient opportunity at that time to introduce this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was just an offer of proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just a moment, please, Mr. Brashich. I had not given you the floor. All right. Proceed, please. Tell us quickly what it is that you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: This is just an offer of proof. It was not meaning that I was trying to argue the case. I was just offering that should an event have taken place, this is what we would have submitted for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, very well. Very well. We have understood. We've understood that if there is a hearing, you will bring in documentary evidence, and I would also say that you're speaking about a document dated 22 May, which is well-known. It's known, and it does not fall within the period that we're talking about because that period stops on the 19th of May, but that doesn't matter. Let me repeat to you, and this is something which is agreed to in all legal systems, that it's not a question of opening the trial now. This is the Pre-Trial phase, and there is no question of opening the door to proofs and counter-proofs in order to establish evidence. This is not the right time. You are in a position where you would know that, because you are high-level counsel. But the question is one of judicial notice. That means either there are facts that are common knowledge and the Trial Chamber will have to then so state, or there are facts which were adjudicated and of which we are taking notice for purposes of judicial economy. Once again, there is no need to go back to the proof of this or that fact. You referred to, for example, the independence which was proclaimed by Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 6th of March. You said that the independence was-- was that independence proclaimed on the legal basis or not? That's not judicial notice. Judicial notice is simply to know whether there was a declaration proclamation. Was there a proclamation or was there not? Do we have to open up that question again? That is in respect of the notion of the proclamation, not an evaluation of the proclamation. I believe that your colleague said that a little while back. You followed it and you said that you would be able to save us some time in this discussion. There is the fact, and there is the conclusion and the evaluation, the interpretation of the fact. If the fact is established under legally judiciously proper conditions in all legal systems, we will take note of that. If it has not been established, we will not take note of that. We cannot decide that it was established, especially if what is involved are controversial evidence as regards the international character of the conflict. There is a problem of classification of the conflict. The Trial Chamber is aware of the importance and the complexity of this issue, and it will deliberate about that knowing fully what it is doing. The last question on this point and then we will end that part of the discussion, one of you, and a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, we would like to know what you mean by "international conflict." It's having been understood if you have a rapid answer that you can give us. It's been understood that we accept as an established fact that there was an armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period in question. Nobody would challenge that. There was a conflict. Now we have to know what you mean by "international conflict." I would like to know, first of all, what the position of the Prosecutor is and then that of the Defence, and then we will put an end to our discussion of that question. Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The definition of international armed conflict can be determined from looking at Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions. In that Article it states, "In addition to the provisions which shall be implemented in peacetime, the present convention shall apply to all cases of declared war or of any other armed conflict which may arise between two or more of the hight-contracting parties even if the state of war is not recognised by one of them. The conventions shall also apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a high-contracting party even if the said occupation meets with no armed resistance." The ICRC commentary to that provision goes on it state that, "Any difference arising between two states and leading to the intervention of members of the armed forces is an armed conflict within the meaning of Article 2." Obviously under the rules of the Geneva Conventions for Article 2 to apply there must be an international armed conflict. So it's our contention that if you have an armed conflict between two or more of the high-contracting parties, and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the SFRY were both high-contracting parties, then you have an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. Paterson. Defence counsel, who would like to speak on that subject? Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I would point to the Court that the United States had a war in 1860. It's still called the Civil War.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, speaking in terms of the high contracting parties in accordance with Geneva Conventions means States. What are the preconditions and prerequisites for one State to be recognised as a State in international terms? To control a territory, the 6th of March and 6th of April and all other further months, around 70 per cent of territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not under the control of Muslim-dominated government in Sarajevo. Without this condition, we cannot speak about the state, ergo there are no high contracting parties, and finally there is no application of Article 2 of Geneva Conventions. To find all this, to make a finding of all this and finding the nexus between the armed forces of one State involved in conflict and military operation on the territory of another State, is the key issue; whether JNA was a power in retreat or it was a power of one State in act of aggression or occupation. All these questions cannot be done between simple discussion and simplification like this. We have to hear well-known experts; we have to hear and to see, more important, highly confidential documents from at least one part in alleged conflict, which was not the case before, here before, all proceedings. We have to hear very shortly some experts on international public law. Just for your reference, in Celebici case, we heard expert Marie-Janine Calic speaking about international character of conflict, only of 20 minutes or half an hour. So in terms of judicial economy, we could provide three experts speaking at least for 45 minutes specifically focused on these issues, and then we could speak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (No interpretation).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the Judge put the microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Pantelic, you've gone back into expert testimony. I'm asking for a specific answer you gave, an answer in respect of what you consider to be an armed conflict. Thank you very much. As regards your oral motion relating to a hearing in order to present evidence about the international nature of the conflict, the Trial Chamber cannot accept it, which means that we will deliberate further to these oral submissions and exchanges between the parties and we will take our decisions. I will now ask you to speak about the second motion, dealing with the establishment of facts; that is, the judicial notice for establishing facts. Mr. Pantelic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As we stated in our response filed yesterday, on Prosecutor's motion for judicial notice or facts of common knowledge, firstly we have to -- well, I have some questions for the Prosecutor bench to explain: How we can consider initial motion for facts of common knowledge? And then is this another motion? The second motion is just an annex to first motion introducing a new term called "adjudicated facts," or we could speak in general about these two motions with regard to one issue. So I would kindly ask my colleagues from Prosecutor bench to give me an answer so that I can focus my discussion or my submission on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: If you can just give me a moment, Your Honour, to reread the transcript so I can understand Mr. Pantelic's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Simply, Ms. Paterson, are we speaking about two separate motions, or one, about one issue, about facts of common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, as we -- as we explained to the Court in our oral argument on this issue, we are of the opinion that the Court can find either/or, that both 94(A) or 94(B) can be applied to these facts. It's our contention that they are all historical facts which are widely accepted by scholars and historians around the world. If the Court does not accept that definition of the facts, then the Court can find them adjudicated facts, because all of the facts listed are facts that have been taken from the decisions of other Trial Chambers before this Tribunal. All of these facts were decided by the Tadic Court and by the Celebici Court, and we would contend that as such, they are adjudicated facts. So that decision, basically, has to be made by the Court, which way they want to classify the fact. We believe they can be classified both ways. It is up to the Court to decide which they think is more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. Paterson. Mr. Pantelic, I hope that you are going to take up the subject, because this has been almost 45 minutes that you are turning around and around the subject, and I will not allow that any further. You have ten minutes to develop the question; ten minutes to tell us what you think about it. Because you are going around and around the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My time is running; okay. So first of all, we did not receive 170 paragraphs of OTP submissions. We only have, in total, 168. So discussion about this very important issue might be very, very delicate, not knowing what is in paragraph 169 and 170. Where the problem is, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, I'm asking you to speak of the 168 paragraphs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But still, it's very important to see in total -- maybe some other important relations between the last two paragraphs might have influence, you know, to maybe discussions about all other. But Your Honour, I will proceed; that's probably a technical question that can be easily resolved with contacts with the registry. So the Defence considers this list of -- I would say hypothetically facts of common knowledge or adjudicated facts -- as a proposal from the Prosecutor's side, fully in accordance with Rule 73 bis, and we consider this annex as an admission or a statement addressed from Prosecutor to the Defence. In light of this, what I said, we are prepared, and we finally state it in our response, that Defence considers non-contested matters of fact as follows, and there are in total I think 60 paragraphs. In our annex 2, we consider the following facts as disputed but non-negotiable; in total, around 12. And finally, in our third annex, this is a statement of Defence, I should be very precise; it's the statement only of counsels for Mr. Milan Simic and Mr. Miroslav Tadic, because unfortunately Mr. Pisarevic was provided by this material only yesterday evening. And finally, we should hear our distinguished colleague Brashich about these issues. In third annex Defence states that we recognise some disputed but negotiable matters of fact. Speaking about these three annexes, and in light and in spirit of cooperation, especially in the interest of justice, and judicial economy, and our clients, Defence is ready to, according to our relief requested in our Defence, in our response, we are ready in a further period to speak and to negotiate with the OTP in order to maybe enlarge this number of facts which could be undisputed between parties, and then we shall have quite precise frame for our further proceedings. In conclusion, Defence considers all these annexes and facts specifically addressed pursuant to Rule 73 bis, and therefore our -- I would like to underline this issue -- our, I would say, statement that we consider some of the facts non-disputed, means that I need another answer from the OTP bench: If, for example, paragraph 56 or the other paragraphs in Tadic judgement or Celebici judgement means that by admission from the Defence side, for example, first paragraph, about the historical issues, means automatically that the Defence is admitted or ready to admit a paragraph from Tadic judgement 56, because Your Honours, if we are reading these paragraphs from Tadic and Celebici judgements, these paragraphs are absolutely controversial. There are many errors, factual misfindings, and all these things. So I would like to stress again, Defence, by admitting these 60 and 4 paragraphs, does not automatically admit that paragraphs from initial judgement. I would like to make it very clear. We admit only formulation from the annex to the Prosecutor motion for adjudicated facts and facts of common knowledge dated February 10th. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. I will summarise, if you agree. Ultimately you have gone back to what is found in the written response. You make a distinction between three categories, which are in the annexes, that the list of facts which you considered as undisputed. I have the text in English here. The second part. You consider those to be disputed, but non-negotiable, and the Trial Chamber will have to make a ruling on that subject. And annex 3, which contains a list of facts which the Defence considers to be disputed but could be the subject of an agreement between the parties. Could I then conclude that you are going to contact the Office of the Prosecutor to discuss the third part, and that you will report back to us on the conclusions that will have led to an agreement between you and the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was our idea, very precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. That concludes our discussion of the second motion dealing with the facts of taking judicial notice on adjudicated facts. Would somebody else like to speak to this issue? I will then move to the third motion and ask the Office of the Prosecutor to speak about the fourth motion for admission of evidence. Ms. Paterson, are you going to speak?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Today seems to be my day to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes. As to the motion requesting admission of documentary evidence, we have brought this to the Court's attention pursuant to Rule 73 and 73 bis, 73 bis dealing with the Pre-Trial conference. Now we acknowledge that in some ways this could be seen as premature, but we have filed this motion in the spirit of the request made to us by Judge Rodrigues to try and resolve as many issues Pre-Trial as possible. The annex of documents constitutes, quite frankly, a majority of the documentary evidence that we intend to introduce at trial although by no means all. There are some additional documents that we may decide to attempt to admit and obviously want to reserve the right to do so at the appropriate time. However, in the spirit of judicial economy, it was our hope that these motions could be accepted into evidence provisionally, with the understanding that we would still be required at trial to authenticate the documents and to establish their relevance, and the Court obviously would rule at that time as to their admissibility and the weight that the Court wants to give the documents. But rather than taking the time during the course of the trial to introduce such a large number of documents one by one, we thought that this was a way to expedite the proceedings. While it would obviously take some time to analyse all the documents, we acknowledge that there is a large number of them; it's our contention that these documents are all relevant to proving motive, intent, knowledge, preparation and planning; that the documents are certainly evidence that goes to support the charges in the indictment, specifically the charges of persecutions and deportations, that they are evidence of the campaign of ethnic cleansing that we allege in the indictment took place in Bosanski Samac and Odzak municipalities as we have noted in our written motion the vast majority of the documents were given to us by officials of government agencies, including officials of the government of Republika Srpska. Almost all of the crisis staff documents that we are asking be admitted were given to us by Mr. Mirko Lukic who is the current mare of Bosanski Samac and was himself a member of the crisis staff during the war. These documents were given to us voluntarily; we did not have to utilise search warrants or subpoenas. In addition the documents relating to the Banja Luka military Court were given to us voluntarily by those government authorities, and in fact many of the documents were also provided by the Defence counsel in this case, by Mr. Pisarevic in particular. So while we realise this may be a somewhat novel approach to this issue, we have decided to at least put it before the Court in an attempt to expedite the proceedings. We are aware that our colleagues in the Omarska case that is also before this Chamber have filed a similar motion, and if Your Honours are willing to accept this approach we think it's a way to expedite the proceedings and move the case along to a trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. Paterson, and thank you for being so concise, which also refers to the written submission that we have before us regarding the admission of documentary evidence and which contains a table listing all those documents, most of which, as you have said, have been conveyed and disclosed to the Defence. Who would like to speak on behalf of the Defence regarding this motion? Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have any particular objections to this motion, so you may consider that we are absolutely agreed upon this way of proceeding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just to make the record clear Your Honour, the only documents on that list that had not yet been disclosed to the Defence are the so-called Banja Luka Military Court documents. I have them in court today and we intend to provide them to Defence before we leave the court today. So at the conclusion of today's proceedings they will have copies of every document on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. Paterson. The Chamber takes note of the fact that all the documents will, at least by the end of the day, all the documents listed will be disclosed to the Defence. We have heard the parties on the four motions submitted by the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm now going to pass on to the second group of motions. Mr. Saint Just?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE SAINT JUST
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, excuse me, regarding the documents that are going to be disclosed by the Prosecution, may I hope that we will have them translated into French in a relatively short delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Madam Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's my understanding that we are under no obligation to translate these documents into French. They are all in English and have also been translated into Serbo-Croatian, but according to my reading of the Rules we are not obligated to also translate them all these documents into French, unless I'm misreading the Rules of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Saint Just, after having studied this question at some depth, it seems that there is a Rule for this type of document in this stage, would have to be provided in only one of the working languages. However, if there's a document, a particular document that you would like to have translated for particular reasons or because of its importance, let the Registrar know and -- or, rather, let the Chamber know and we will let the Registrar know to have it translated. This also applies to us, because we often have to work in English even though our language is French, and sometimes we need to request further clarification. So that is the approach. Thank you, Mr. De Saint Just. I'm now going to -- the Chamber wishes now to proceed with the motion submitted by the Defence, and as I announced this morning, among all these motions, most of them concern the accused Todorovic. There are about 15 of them -- or 15 precisely, and I would suggest in this case too that we group them according to what they have in common. So we will begin with the motion regarding evidence, and then we will go on to hear the parties regarding the form of the indictment. Then the first regarding evidence, we have grouped five such motions, the motion for discovery -- I apologise for using the English words because I have the text in English -- the production of material, motion for production of witness statements, the motion to exclude testimony from the accused, motion to suppress identification, and the fifth, the motion to strike and exclude testimony. These are five motions which have to do with evidence, and that is why we have put them in one category. Therefore, if the Defence agrees, Mr. Brashich, will you be so kind as to argue them in that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: As to the characterisation, and at least I think with regard to my end, this will be a briefer exercise than before. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Initially one of the defences to these motions, which I would like to lay to rest, was the issue of untimeliness. The way I read the scheduling order is that it had a particular date. My understanding as to dates, it's not close of business, it is 12.00. My motions were timely filed before the end of my working day. In any event, before 12.00 midnight Hague time. And I will note that with regard to responses, when I left at 5.00, which I believe is the close of the working day of the court, there was nothing in my locker, but when I arrived this morning at 9.00 I had the responses from the Prosecutor. My inquiry of the Registrar was that apparently 8.00 was when they were received from the Prosecutor. Your Honour, these are very pro forma motions which seek to flush out anything which might have been omitted either by error or by omission by the Prosecutor in fulfilling her responsibility under the Rules. With regard to the motion for production of discovery and exculpatory information, this is the standard request made upon a Prosecutor that any information contained in the Prosecutor's files should be made available to the Defence. I'm used to something which is called an open file Prosecution where I can walk into the Prosecutor's office and physically go through the Prosecutor's file. I do not have that situation here, and, therefore, I have requested with specificity documents which I do not say exist, which I state might exist, and if they do exist I wish to have them made available to me. I have read the Defence -- the Prosecution's opposition to my omnibus application, and I have noted that certain categories of information which I had requested do not exist. They are withdrawn, Your Honour. With regard to the ones that are not -- there are some which are not applicable. I withdraw those also. With regard to the compliance to certain requests, there has been some compliance and the answers note that there will be further compliance. With regard to those, Your Honour, I would simply, since there are no time limitations under the Rules, reserve the right to move again in a timely fashion prior to trial if compliance has not been had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Brashich. If I understood you well, you have already taken note of the fact that some of the documents that you are asking for do not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, in one example, in the answer of the Prosecutor for a document which I had requested, which is a statement of the defendant, the Prosecution makes and warrants to the Court that no statements were made by my client. Now, I do know that when my client was arrested that there were certain statements made, but if the Prosecution states that there are no statements, so be it. That is the kind of a situation which I was referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich, are there any specific documents outside the fact that you reserve the right to intervene later on, any specific document that you're requesting from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I believe that some of the documents which I had requested would fall within the motion as to the arrest and detention of my client, and I suppose with regard to those specific documents that can be deferred to another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Very well. That goes without saying, because you have asked that these motions be discussed in the presence of the whole Chamber. Perhaps we will be able to do that tomorrow if Judge May is better. Therefore, for the moment, as far as I understand, you have nothing to request. Ms. Paterson, would you wish to comment on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could first just clarify the record. The Prosecutor's office filed all of its motions at 5.20 yesterday afternoon, which is before the close of business which we have been instructed is 5.30 Hague time. So I don't know where Mr. Brashich got the information that we filed them at 8.00 p.m., but they were filed at 5.20, which we realise was at the end of the day but, nonetheless, was within the necessary time. As to this statement that Mr. Todorovic may or may not have made at the time of his arrest, if such a statement was made, it apparently was some sort of an oral statement either to representatives of SFOR or perhaps to an investigator of the Tribunal. No such statement has ever been brought to our attention. I certainly am not aware of any written statement made by Mr. Todorovic. As we've pointed out in our responses, on the 10th of February I had a discussion with Mr. Brashich in which I expressed an interest on the part of our office in speaking with Mr. Todorovic, and he said that he would get back to me. So clearly we have not, ourselves, taken a statement yet from Mr. Todorovic that we have to disclose. If Your Honours would like us to respond orally to these basically what I see are nine motions, if we do not count the severance and arrest motions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: -- we are prepared to do so, but, frankly, I think that we can pretty much stand by our written responses. We really have nothing of any substance to add beyond what we've put in our written responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. For the moment we're dealing with the motion to compel production of discovery and exculpatory information. I think we have clarified the situation for the moment as far as that is concerned, with the right of Mr. Brashich to request documents when we come to the motion on the arrest. Therefore, Mr. Brashich, you have the floor if you wish now to comment on the other motions that I have cited a moment ago regarding evidence, the motion that you submitted, motion for the production of statements, motion to exclude testimony from the accused, motion to suppress identification, and motion to strike and exclude testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to most of these motions, I agree with Ms. Paterson that the written submissions are more than adequate, and I think that the Court, in due course, can take care of it. The two motions which I would like to address orally is we have, during discovery, been given a great number of witness statements. Now, the way that these witness statements were prepared was with an interpreter, an investigator and transcribed. With regard to witness statements, what I had asked was for an order directing the Prosecutor to give us any written notes made by the investigator or the person conducting the interview which were contemporaneous with such interview. I think that that is a fair subject for exploration by the Defence during any cross-examination, and that would flush out any discrepancies between any written witness statements and what actually was taking place during the interviews. The only other motion that I would propose to address the Court orally would be the motion to strike the aliases from the indictment. I recognise that this court and this Trial Chamber is a highly sophisticated, and erudite and experienced Trial Chamber, and that it can disregard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just a moment, please, Mr. Brashich. I should like us to finish first with the question of the motions concerning evidence. Have you finished with that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: -- any contemporaneous notes taken by investigators or the persons interviewed of the individuals with regard to the disclosed witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Brashich. Ms. Paterson, do you wish to intervene on this the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarifying the record while we're all present, Mr. Brashich has a misunderstanding of how we conduct our interviews in the field. As Your Honours can understand particularly when we are interviewing witnesses in the former Yugoslavia, and when we were interviewing witnesses while the war was going on we were working under difficult circumstances. Generally what we do is an investigator sits down with a laptop computer, as best they can they type the statement simultaneously while it is being taken. They discuss it with the witness to make sure that it's accurate. A final version is then produced and read to the witness and signed and confirmed by the witness. For the most part of the investigators do not take contemporaneous notes. They do not sit and take handwritten notes and then type them. Usually they are typing at the same time they are conducting the interview. There are some exceptions to that, as to investigators who are not fluent in English who take it in their own language and then transfer it into English for purposes of the statement, but it is the policy of the OTP that all such notes, for confidentiality and security reasons, since we are operating in the field, all such notes and all notes that any interpreters may take are shredded and destroyed and are not saved by the Office of the Prosecutor. So to my knowledge, there are no such contemporaneous notes to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Brashich, do you wish to give us additional information about the rest of the motions? After all, you submitted 11. There are five concerning evidence, then the two following ones on which I should like to hear you, if you have anything to add having to do with the form of the indictment. That is a motion for a bill of particulars, and the motion that we have already started discussing, to strike aliases attached to the name, to strike the nicknames. These are two motions regarding the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In regard to the bill of particulars, Your Honour, as I alluded this morning, I am still a novice with the Rules of this Court, even though I have read them and keep rereading them. Perhaps Ms. Paterson is correct that my motion for a bill of particulars is premature, inasmuch as I had not made a formal demand for the information sought by that motion. If that be so, then I apologise to the Court, and with regard to the bill of particulars, I will withdraw it. I will make the appropriate demand upon Ms. Paterson, and should she fail to comply, we'll be back in front of you. For that taking up of the time and with regard to my noncompliance with the Rules, I apologise. With regard to the motion for aliases, I had spoken that this chamber is experienced, sophisticated, and may easily overlook the opprobrium which is contained in the aliases. But just to seem -- not to have the Chamber have what I think is an improper reference to the defendant, who still is only the accused, I would request that my application be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Brashich. Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason that the aliases were put in the indictment at the outset of the case was because those are the names by which the defendant is referred to by many of our witnesses. Some of them refer to him as Mr. Todorovic; some only knew him by the nicknames that are listed there: Stiv, Stevo, or Monstrum. Whether Mr. Brashich or Mr. Todorovic like it or not, he was known by the nickname of Monstrum, and many of our witnesses will testify to that, that that is how they knew him. Because under the circumstances that was the only, in some cases, name that they could provide to us, it was a name that we thought was appropriate to put in the indictment. As we said in our motion, we have confidence in this Court that they will not be swayed by any such names in your determination of the facts of the case, and we will be certainly glad to abide by the ruling of the Court on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Ms. Paterson. Judge Robinson? I consulted with my colleague. As regards firstly the clarifications that were made in the indictment, that is, the motion for a bill of particulars, I note what Mr. Brashich said; that is, that the motion for the time being is not current, and that we are waiting for clarifications from the Office of the Prosecutor in due course. And therefore the Trial Chamber requests that the Prosecutor, after having contacted the Defence, see what clarification should be added to the Pre-Trial stage. As regards the nicknames, we do not think that it is really necessary to put them into an indictment. If the witnesses come and use nicknames, they can always state that during testimony. Having said that, obviously in no case can these nicknames influence our judgement or our choices. That is what we have to say about the two motions dealing with the form of the indictment and the issue of the nicknames. We now have remaining to us the remaining motions, which you filed, Mr. Brashich. There is a motion which you called "Motion for the OTP to elect the theory of prosecution"; another which you have called "Motion for an evidentiary hearing regarding the nature of the conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I think that that is no longer on our agenda for this afternoon, since we settled that issue a while back. And another motion, which you requested be left until a full bench of Judges can deal with it: That is the severance of the accused. And you were speaking for Mr. Todorovic. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. With regard to the motion for an evidentiary hearing as to the nature of the conflict, we've done that. With regard to the motion to elect a theory, I have read the response of the Prosecution; I now see their theory, and in that -- as being "a continuing course of conduct," and I'm putting that in quotes. And I think that with regard to that issue, the papers as submitted are more than adequate, and the Court will decide whether or not the position taken by the Prosecutor as to alternate theories is one which should be allowed or denied. And I believe I'm missing one of the motions that the Court mentioned, and then -- after a while they all seem to look alike, Your Honour. The last one, Your Honour, I believe that the Court mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are you looking for the motion to elect theory of prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe both of those are different -- or the other side of the face with regards to elect. So those two motions really should be submitted as one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACFADYEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the only issue that I believe my friend has indicated is still outstanding, and that is the ability or not of the Prosecutor to lay in the indictment alternative charges, I would direct Your Honours to paragraph 14 in the Prosecution's response to the elect theory or dismiss motion, where it indicates that the Court -- Tribunal, sorry, and Prosecutor group in Blaskic found that nothing prevents the Prosecutor from pleading an alternative responsibility, Article 7 sub (1), or Article 7 sub (3) of the statute, but the factual allegations supporting either alternative must be sufficiently precise so as to permit the accused to prepare his defence on either or both alternatives. The citation was from April 1997 in the decision on the Defence motion to dismiss the indictment based on defects in the form thereof. This was in the Blaskic case. I believe my friend has indicated that in fact as a result of the -- possibly paragraph 7, 8, and 9 in the response to his motion, he is now able to tell by reading the indictment, because it relates to how the law is set out here, what actions Mr. Todorovic is liable for individually, as a superior, or because he participated in a group event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Since I've only received the answers this morning, I am not familiar with the Celebici decision on the motion, and I would stand on my written request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I think, Mr. Brashich, that we have heard a discussion about all of the motions that you have filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Does somebody else have anything to say about the Defence motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: With regard to the motions, Your Honour? Or any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes. No, I'm talking about the motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. I therefore consider that our Trial Chamber has heard the pleadings about these motions except for two, and that was at your request, and they will be reviewed, hopefully, tomorrow afternoon. There is a session which is scheduled in this Trial Chamber tomorrow at 2.00. And we hope that Judge May will be with us. If not, we will meet anyway in order to reach a decision on the agenda, the schedule for the remaining period. And now I ask whether anyone has anything else to add in general. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with regard to the motion as to the conflict, Defence counsel requested from the Registrar a joint conference where all counsel would be present together with the defendants so that the conflict could be discussed and the conflict could also be made known to the accused. When we got to the detention facilities, I was apprised that the Registrar's Office was going to tape the Defence conference, and that it was the -- the Registrar was going to have an individual sit in to the Defence conference. I'm well aware that by having a joint Defence meeting waivers of attorney-client privileges occur. However, I was appalled that the Registrar had the temerity, or the affront, to tape a conference amongst Defence attorneys and their counsel on an issue that is joint. My request, Your Honour, with regard to that, and this is a speaking motion, that in the future, that there be any joint meetings of Defence counsel and their clients, that the Registrar be directed not to tape such a meeting, and not to have an individual present. My second request is that any tape and copies of the meeting had Monday morning be destroyed, and number three, an order to the Registrar asking whether or not the tape of the Defence counsel was disclosed to any third parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Brashich. Mr. Pisarevic? Are you going to speak about the same subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I agree with what Mr. Brashich has said. I have one, however, suggestion to make. Mr. Brashich mentioned this meeting that we had, and we discussed the conflicts of interest at that meeting. The conflicts of interest which is being addressed here upon the motion of the Prosecutor. I wish to suggest to the Honourable Chamber that in view of the complexity of the issue and the position of my client and the situation he has found himself as a result of this, that here before your Chamber all of the accused state their position for the record, and state whether in their opinion there is a potential conflict of interest. And I think that we should use this opportunity now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm going to consult the Legal Officer and the representative of the Registrar. As regards Point 1, Mr. Brashich, having to do with that meeting, I am learning from you about what happened on during that joint meeting. Believe me, I've just learned this as well. Therefore we are going to stop for a few moments and going to take a 20-minute break. The time necessary in order to hear the representative of the Registry on that issue, because you are informing us of a type of behaviour that we must be aware of, and we will resume the session, shall we say, at ten after 4.00; it's now about ten to 4.00, we'll starts again in 20 minutes, at ten after 4.00. As regards the seconds question that was asked by Mr. Pisarevic, having to do with the conflict of interest, you say that -- you ask whether these accused cannot be asked whether they feel that there's a conflict of interest. Listen, speak about that among yourselves, Defence counsel with their accused, and we'll go back to that issue tomorrow. The Trial Chamber is prepared to hear the accuseds' feeling on the question of a conflict of interest. We might have a meeting tomorrow; that would leave you the time to explain the question to the accused -- and detail because the question is not a simple one, so that they be well aware of the issue before you come to speak before the Trial Chamber. Therefore at 2.00 tomorrow, we will hear what they have to say, and we will speak about the schedule, and I hope that if Judge May's health permits us to do so, we will deal with the pending motions. We will take a 20-minute break now -- just one moment, please. There's no change. All right. It will be a closed session and the minutes will be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: 4:45 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of March, 1999, at 2.30 p.m.
